subject: math
cluster: Draw, construct, and describe geometrical figures and describe the relationships between them
skillName: Draw, construct, and describe geometrical figures and describe the relationships between them
intro: This cluster worksheet covers all three standards in the geometry cluster 7.G.A: solving problems with scale drawings (7.G.A.1), drawing and classifying geometric shapes from given conditions (7.G.A.2), and identifying cross sections of three-dimensional figures (7.G.A.3). Items are grouped by standard and ramp in difficulty from straightforward to multi-step.

items.prompt: A map uses the scale $1\text{ cm} : 6\text{ km}$. Two towns are $5\text{ cm}$ apart on the map. What is the actual distance between the towns?

steps: Each $1\text{ cm}$ on the map stands for $6\text{ km}$ of real distance.
Multiply the map distance by the scale: $5 \times 6 = 30$.
The actual distance is $30\text{ km}$.

items.prompt: A blueprint uses the scale $1\text{ in} : 4\text{ ft}$. A wall is $18\text{ ft}$ long. How long is the wall on the blueprint?

steps: Going from actual length to drawing length, divide by the scale factor of $4$.
Compute $\frac{18}{4} = 4.5$.
The wall is $4.5\text{ in}$ long on the blueprint.

items.prompt: On a scale drawing, a segment is $3\text{ cm}$ long and represents an actual length of $15\text{ m}$. Write the scale in the form $1\text{ cm} : ?\text{ m}$.

steps: The scale compares drawing length to actual length: $3\text{ cm} : 15\text{ m}$.
Divide both quantities by $3$ to make the drawing side equal $1\text{ cm}$: $\frac{3}{3}\text{ cm} : \frac{15}{3}\text{ m}$.
This gives the scale $1\text{ cm} : 5\text{ m}$.

items.prompt: A rectangular garden is drawn $4\text{ cm}$ by $6\text{ cm}$ using the scale $1\text{ cm} : 3\text{ m}$. Find the actual area of the garden.

steps: Find the actual length and width. Length: $6 \times 3 = 18\text{ m}$. Width: $4 \times 3 = 12\text{ m}$.
Compute the actual area: $18 \times 12 = 216$.
The actual area is $216\text{ m}^2$. (Check: drawing area $4 \times 6 = 24\text{ cm}^2$ times the squared scale factor $3^2 = 9$ gives $24 \times 9 = 216\text{ m}^2$.)

items.prompt: A figure is drawn at the scale $1\text{ cm} : 2\text{ m}$, and one of its sides measures $5\text{ cm}$. The figure is to be redrawn at the scale $1\text{ cm} : 5\text{ m}$. How long is that side in the new drawing?

steps: First find the actual length of the side using the original scale: $5 \times 2 = 10\text{ m}$.
Now apply the new scale, where $1\text{ cm}$ represents $5\text{ m}$, so divide the actual length by $5$.
Compute $\frac{10}{5} = 2$.
In the new drawing the side measures $2\text{ cm}$.

items.prompt: Can a triangle be drawn with side lengths $4\text{ cm}$, $5\text{ cm}$, and $11\text{ cm}$? Explain using the triangle inequality.
items.answer: No, a triangle cannot be drawn.

steps: By the triangle inequality, the sum of the two shorter sides must be greater than the longest side.
Add the two shorter sides: $4 + 5 = 9$.
Compare to the longest side: $9 < 11$.
Since the sum is not greater than the longest side, no triangle can be drawn.

items.prompt: Can a triangle have interior angles measuring $40^\circ$, $60^\circ$, and $90^\circ$? Explain.
items.answer: No, those angles cannot form a triangle.

steps: The three interior angles of any triangle must sum to exactly $180^\circ$.
Add the given angles: $40 + 60 + 90 = 190$.
Since $190^\circ \ne 180^\circ$, these three angles cannot form a triangle.

items.prompt: A triangle is given by two sides of $6\text{ cm}$ and $8\text{ cm}$ with the included angle of $40^\circ$ between them. Does this determine a unique triangle, more than one triangle, or no triangle? Name the congruence criterion that applies.
items.answer: A unique triangle; the criterion is SAS.

steps: Two sides and the angle between them are given. The given angle is the included angle.
When two sides and the included angle are fixed, the third side and the figure are completely determined.
This is the SAS (side-angle-side) criterion, which always produces a unique triangle.

items.prompt: Three angle measures $50^\circ$, $60^\circ$, and $70^\circ$ are given for a triangle, with no side length specified. Does this determine a unique triangle, more than one triangle, or no triangle? Justify your answer.

steps: First check feasibility: $50 + 60 + 70 = 180^\circ$, so a triangle with these angles is possible.
Only the three angles are fixed; no side length is given. This is the AAA condition.
AAA fixes the shape but not the size, so triangles of many different sizes all satisfy the conditions.
Therefore more than one triangle (in fact infinitely many similar triangles) can be drawn.

items.prompt: In a triangle, two of the angles measure $35^\circ$ and $85^\circ$, and the side between these two angles is $9\text{ cm}$ long. Find the third angle, then state whether the conditions determine a unique triangle and name the congruence criterion.
items.answer: Third angle $= 60^\circ$; a unique triangle by ASA.

steps: Use the angle-sum property: the third angle is $180 - 35 - 85 = 60^\circ$.
The given $9\text{ cm}$ side lies between the $35^\circ$ and $85^\circ$ angles, so two angles and the included side are fixed.
Two angles and the included side determine a unique triangle. This is the ASA (angle-side-angle) criterion.
So the conditions give exactly one triangle, with angles $35^\circ$, $85^\circ$, and $60^\circ$.

items.prompt: A right rectangular prism is $6\text{ cm}$ long, $4\text{ cm}$ wide, and $3\text{ cm}$ tall. A plane slices the prism parallel to its top and bottom faces. What two-dimensional figure is the cross section, and what are its dimensions?
items.answer: A rectangle measuring $6\text{ cm}$ by $4\text{ cm}$.

steps: A slice parallel to the top and bottom faces produces a cross section congruent to those faces.
The top and bottom faces are formed by the length and width: $6\text{ cm}$ by $4\text{ cm}$.
The cross section is a rectangle measuring $6\text{ cm}$ by $4\text{ cm}$.

items.prompt: A right rectangular pyramid is sliced by a vertical plane that passes through the apex and is parallel to one pair of base edges. What two-dimensional figure is the cross section?

steps: A slice through the apex reaches down to the base, meeting the base in a line segment.
The plane meets two lateral faces along edges that run from that base segment up to the single apex point.
Three line segments (the base segment and the two edges meeting at the apex) bound the region, so the cross section is a triangle.

items.prompt: A right rectangular prism measures $8\text{ in}$ by $5\text{ in}$ by $2\text{ in}$. A vertical plane cuts straight down perpendicular to the $8\text{ in}$ length, exposing a face whose dimensions are the width and the height. Name the cross section and find its area.
items.answer: A rectangle measuring $5\text{ in}$ by $2\text{ in}$, with area $10\text{ in}^2$.

steps: A vertical cut perpendicular to the $8\text{ in}$ length exposes the other two dimensions: the width $5\text{ in}$ and the height $2\text{ in}$.
The cross section is a rectangle measuring $5\text{ in}$ by $2\text{ in}$.
Its area is $5 \times 2 = 10\text{ in}^2$.

items.prompt: A right rectangular pyramid has a base $10\text{ ft}$ by $6\text{ ft}$. A plane slices it parallel to the base exactly halfway up the height. Name the cross section and give its dimensions.
items.answer: A rectangle measuring $5\text{ ft}$ by $3\text{ ft}$.

steps: A slice parallel to the base of a pyramid is similar to the base, so the cross section is a rectangle.
At half the height, each linear dimension of the cross section is $\frac{1}{2}$ of the base dimension.
Length: $10 \times \frac{1}{2} = 5\text{ ft}$. Width: $6 \times \frac{1}{2} = 3\text{ ft}$.
The cross section is a rectangle measuring $5\text{ ft}$ by $3\text{ ft}$.

items.prompt: A right rectangular pyramid is cut by a plane that is not parallel to the base and does not pass through the apex, but is parallel to one pair of base edges and intersects all four lateral faces. A student claims the cross section is a rectangle. Name the actual cross section and explain why the student is wrong.
items.answer: A trapezoid; the student is wrong because the tilted cut makes the two parallel-cut edges sit at different heights on the narrowing pyramid, so they have unequal lengths.

steps: The plane crosses all four lateral faces, so the cross section is a four-sided figure (a quadrilateral).
Because the slice is parallel to one pair of base edges, the two sides of the section that lie on the faces containing those edges are parallel.
Because the slice is tilted (not parallel to the base) and the pyramid narrows toward the apex, those two parallel sides occur at different heights and have different lengths.
A quadrilateral with exactly one pair of parallel sides of unequal length is a trapezoid, not a rectangle, so the student's claim is incorrect.
